title: Living with Ubiquitous Sensors
text:
Cities are increasingly saturated with sensors that record traffic, air quality and the movements of their residents. Planners praise these systems for reducing congestion and anticipating failures in infrastructure. Yet the same data can quietly reveal where people live, work and worship, which makes the question of consent difficult to answer.

Privacy advocates therefore argue that data collection should be limited by purpose, not merely by technical capacity. Others contend that anonymised datasets offer a reasonable compromise, although researchers have shown that supposedly anonymous records can often be re-identified. The debate, in essence, concerns who decides what a city is permitted to know about its inhabitants.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do planners praise these sensor systems for?
options: Reducing congestion and anticipating infrastructure failures
Collecting data about private religious beliefs only

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what have researchers shown about anonymised records?
options: They can never be linked to individuals
Supposedly anonymous records can often be re-identified
They are used only by planners

questions.text: Why does the passage describe the question of consent as difficult to answer?
options: Because residents do not own any data
Because the same data can reveal sensitive details about people's lives
Because sensors do not work in cities

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the position of privacy advocates?
options: They believe technical capacity should decide what is collected
They believe purpose should limit data collection
They oppose all use of urban data
They think anonymised data is entirely safe
